subject: Stabilization fee charged to an HOA Harvard Oaks PUD / D6
comment: Hi Jesse and Councilman Dugan I just tried to talk to the SLC Water to gain a detailed understanding of the stabilization fee and was told "call your City Councilman". I'm was looking for hard information and if there is a web site, I'm happy to take the time to read. In short, here is the impetus to why I'm looking for information: our HOA needs to make a dramatic increase in our monthly fee and a special assessment based on this new stabilization rate. Here is the situation and my questions: 1) We live in a 10 home PUD and we pay our water and sewer bill within the HOA assessment. 2) Apparently rather than each home having an individual water meter, when they developed the property, they did so under one water meter. The development was created in the 1980s and not sure if it was part of the development agreement or if it was done to save connection fees. 3) Apparently when the City allowed the property to be developed, the City required the HOA be responsible to care for the area along the parking strip beyond the "homes" area, next to a creek along 2100 East. We pay to landscape and water this land. Water that is measured through this same meter, even though no homes receive benefit. Question: how long is the HOA obligated to take care of this area? Would it be possible to turn its care and watering responsibility back to the City? 4) Our actual improved landscaping within the HOA is much less than the normal single family residence, but because of the 10 homes on one meter, we are put in the large users category and adversely financially affected due to the large size of the meter. The person on the call simply told me "your HOA was notified in May and should have gone to the City Council Meeting and voiced their opinion". I do not sit on the board, but even if I had been at the council meeting, our situation may not have been considered. I do not understand that the pipes need to be maintained and there is a cost associated. And I'm sure you are intelligent, reasonable people who have the capacity to understand the point that we have 10 homes on this large meter. Does it make sense that Harvard Oaks Association homeowners have a greater financial impact than other single family users when our footprint is actually smaller than the normal single family lot size? I welcome being educated if I do not understand your solution. I am happy to attend a meeting or zoom call with you and other members of the HOA. -- Vickey Walker

subject: Comments on the SEG Participation Agreement
comment: Hi Councilmembers, My name is Eric Valchuis and I am a resident of District 6 and I own a business that is located in District 4 (Baby's Bagels). I am writing to make some comments regarding the Sports and Entertainment District. I support the revitalization of this area. From an urban planning perspective, this area of town, with its long blocks, wide streets, and in-active ground-floor uses, make it an area where I do not typically choose to spend time. Accordingly, I support the rezoning that was approved this week. I support the use of public funds to accomplish this revitalization. Public funds are known to catalyze the revitalization of neighborhoods. As such, I support public dollars being spent to improve this area. I do not support using public funds to renovate the Delta Center. From my understanding of the Participation Agreement, Salt Lakers will see their sales taxes increase to raise $900M for SEG to spend. The majority of that money ($525M) will go towards the renovation of the Delta Center. Reason and research show that the renovation of arenas do not meaningfully contribute towards the revitalization of a larger area. Ryan Smith--owner of SEG--is quoted as saying, "Our efforts are not about an arena, it's about revitalizing a downtown that desperately needs investment." This statement does not match the impact of the Participation Agreement. As such, I hope that a different arrangement can be negotiated. Thanks for hearing out my views and for all of your work. Eric Valchuis

subject: Conditional Use for Concrete Manufacturing Facility @ About 1055 N Warm Springs Road
comment: Dear City Council Members: I am writing to oppose the Conditional Use Permit for a Concrete Manufacturing Facility at Approximately 1055 N Warm Springs Road that comes up for consideration on September 11 at 5:30 PM. The area is now zoned for light manufacturing. The proposed concrete manufacturing facility would put within the boundaries of Salt Lake City a plant that would add considerably to our air pollution problems. This type of plant is known to be a very significant source of fine and coarse particulates, in this case it is part of the project that would include the quarry/mine proposed for Parleys Canyon, a mine opposed by Salt Lake City and Salt Lake County but which appears to have the blessings of the Utah State Government. We have enough problems trying to meet EPA standards for air quality and the mine plus this proposed concrete manufacturing facility would add to our already high PM levels at both the eastern and western sides of our city. These particulates threaten the health and well-being of our citizens. I am a retired physician that specializes in diseases of the lung including those caused by environmental factors. I have published research papers on this topic and served on the Utah State Air Quality Board and was the Chair of this board in my final 2 years of service. Please reject this application for the sake of all of our citizens. Thank you. Sincerely, Richard E. Kanner, MD

subject: RDA - Disposition Update for Property at 167-169 South Regent Street
comment: Good day SLC Council: I am writing to you regarding your role as the RDA Board. On Aug 13 you received a written briefing on the Disposition Update for Property at 167-169 South Regent Street. I would like to submit public comment on this topic. In reading a Building Salt Lake article (https://buildingsaltlake.com/cw-urban-planning-to-build-a-new-condo-tower-on-regent-street/) about this topic, it is my understanding that a developer, CW Urban, plans to purchase RDA parcels on Regent Street to combine with other parcels owned by Dakota Pacific, in order to build a new development. Looking at the SL County Assessor site, I see that Dakota Pacific currently owns the historic Felt Electric Building and another parcel. As the briefing to the RDA was not public, it is difficult to know the exact plans. But it is reasonable to surmise that these parcels along the south end of Regent Street (165, 167, 169 Regent and 42 E 200 S) may all be combined for a new development. My specific concern is the fate of the historic Felt Electric Building at 165 S Regent St. This building is listed on the National Register of Historic Places (NRHP) but is not a local historic landmark site. In brief, the history of the building is significant and is the last remaining building of the old SLC tenderloin district that once included Regent St (previously Commercial St), Plum Alley (Chinatown), and Victoria Alley (now Gallivan Center). Although built by a respectable SLC businessman who also owned the famed Knutsford Hotel (demolished), it was built specifically to accommodate prostitution on the top floors while presenting a respectable business on the ground floor. It is representative of SLC multi-faced personality when it comes to the history of vices. And it is rather amazing that it still stands and is in great condition, with several recent tenants. The SHPO file on the history of the building can be accessed here: https://collections.lib.utah.edu/ark:/87278/s6vn0554 I urge you in your role as RDA officials to in some way mandate the preservation of the historic Felt Electric Building as part of any deal regarding the Disposition of Property at 167-169 Regent Street, development of said parcels, and/or request to combine parcels. Something similar to what was done with the Cramer House downtown. Clearly, this is subject to legal review but if there is a legal avenue to accommodate such a requirement I believe it would benefit the future of the City. very respectfully, Rachel Quist
